content: The combination of Brahmabuti, Centella Asiatica, and Hydrocotyle Gotu Kola is used for various indications, with specific dosing regimens depending on the condition being treated. Oral dosing includes 60 mg taken twice to three times daily, 600 mg taken three times daily, or 1 cup of tea prepared with 600 mg of dried leaves in 150 ml of water, consumed three times daily. Topical application involves the use of a 1% cream applied daily. This combination is possibly effective for conditions such as abdominal disorders, aphrodisiac purposes, common cold or flu, fatigue, memory enhancement, varicose veins, and venous insufficiency. Topical uses include hypertrophic scarring, psoriasis, and wound healing. Gotu Kola has pharmacodynamic interactions with several medications, enhancing their effects through synergism. These include amobarbital, azelastine, brompheniramine, butabarbital, butalbital, carbinoxamine, chloral hydrate, chlorpheniramine, cinnarizine, clemastine, cyclizine, cyproheptadine, dexchlorpheniramine, dexmedetomidine, dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, hydroxyzine, pentobarbital, phenobarbital, primidone, promethazine, triclophos, and triprolidine. These interactions may enhance central nervous system (CNS) depression, necessitating caution and close monitoring. Additionally, Gotu Kola may theoretically enhance the effects of antidiabetic agents such as acarbose, glimepiride, glipizide, glyburide, insulin (aspart, detemir, glargine, glulisine, lispro, NPH, and regular human), metformin, miglitol, nateglinide, pioglitazone, repaglinide, rosiglitazone, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, and vildagliptin. These interactions are considered minor, with unknown clinical significance, and are based on theoretical mechanisms. Adverse effects associated with Gotu Kola include gastrointestinal upset, nausea, photosensitivity, and pruritus. Topical use may cause allergic contact dermatitis and burning sensations. Large doses can lead to drowsiness, hypercholesterolemia, hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and sedation. Contraindications include concurrent use with sedative agents, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia. Use during pregnancy and lactation is not recommended, as it falls under the category of avoid use. However, in general, controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
